Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.23571.question: In Transformer experiments, how does BMuon compare with Muon and other baselines on post-training pruning, model quality, and training cost at matched settings?

passages.text: Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

To summarize, our main contributions are: • We introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which incorporates a single global hidden-channel budget into Muon’s spectral update geometry, while coupling the matrix slices that define each MLP channel. • We characterize the induced norm family Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} and its relation to Muon and structured sparse geometries in Section 2 . In the linear factorization setting of Section 3 , we show that for a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost is also attained by redundant-width factorizations. • We derive a practical minorization–maximization surrogate for the global allocation problem, yielding a tractable allocation update in Section 4 . • In Section 5 , we show across CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model that BMuon improves structured MLP-channel compressibility relative to Muon. In the vision experiments, the learned allocations also provide effective pruning scores and identify non-uniform MLP architectures that outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and a global budget over all 4608 MLP hidden channels. The budget is linearly annealed from 4608 to 922, corresponding approximately to 20 % 20\% of the total channel mass, over the first third of training and then held fixed. The allocation is updated every five optimizer steps using one MM update, with ε = 10 − 6 \varepsilon=10^{-6} . Non-MLP Transformer matrices use ordinary Muon. Muon+GL. Muon+GL applies an exact proximal Group-Lasso step with coefficient λ GL \lambda_{\mathrm{GL}} to coupled MLP hidden-channel groups ( W 1 , j : ℓ , W 2 , : , j ℓ ) (W^{\ell}_{1,j:},W^{\ell}_{2,:,j}) , using the group norm ( ∥ W 1 , j : ℓ ∥ 2 2 + ∥ W 2 , : , j ℓ ∥ 2 2 ) 1 / 2 \bigl(\|W^{\ell}_{1,j:}\|_{2}^{2}+\|W^{\ell}_{2,:,j}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} . We tune λ GL ∈ { 0.01 , 0.02 , 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.5 } \lambda_{\mathrm{GL}}\in\{0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5\} , obtaining mean dense accuracies of 71.50, 71.58, 71.25, 70.03, 69.23, and 61.21%, respectively. Increasing λ GL \lambda_{\mathrm{GL}} strengthens the sparsity-inducing penalty and can improve post-training compressibility at the expense of dense accuracy. To compare at similar pre-compression accuracy, we restrict attention here to settings within one percentage point of BMuon’s 71.46 % 71.46\% , leaving λ GL ∈ { 0.01 , 0.02 , 0.05 } \lambda_{\mathrm{GL}}\in\{0.01,0.02,0.05\} . At 50 % 50\% MLP-channel pruning, these settings retain 9.71 % 9.71\% , 16.30 % 16.30\% , and 71.25 % 71.25\% test accuracy, respectively. We therefore use λ GL = 0.05 \lambda_{\mathrm{GL}}=0.05 throughout this experiment.

Our LLaMA/FineWeb experiments are based on the LLaMA-1B setup of Muon+ ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) 1 1 1 https://github.com/K1seki221/MuonPlus . We adopt its architecture and training recipe, reducing only the number of Transformer blocks from 24 24 to 17 17 to obtain a 986,746,880 986{,}746{,}880 -parameter model; all other architectural hyperparameters are unchanged. The Muon+ codebase builds on Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and the modded-nanogpt training framework 2 2 2 https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt . We retain its LLaMA-2 tokenizer and FineWeb preprocessing and sharding conventions, Muon parameter routing, auxiliary AdamW-style updates for non-Muon parameters, momentum/Nesterov convention, five-step Newton–Schulz polar approximation, matrix learning-rate shape/RMS scaling, warmup–cosine schedule, and BF16 training conventions. For our experiments, we integrate BMuon into the SwiGLU MLPs.

inspect:2610.22794.question: In the 1B LLaMA pretraining experiments, how does Ori compare with GaLore and full-rank optimizers at matched rank and training budget on validation loss, peak GPU memory, and training throughput?

passages.text: We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

We used a variety of compute resources with different GPU hardware, including RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti Super, RTX A500, RTX A6000, 40GB A100, 80GB A100, H100, MI100, and MI210. For the large model pre-training, such as the 350M and 1B LLaMA model pre-training experiments, we trained the model on nodes equipped with 4 H100 or 4 MI210.

passages.section: E.8 Measuring optimizer state peak memory
passages.text: Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

Table 9 : Memory and Wallclock Time Comparison between Ori and non-error-feedback baselines (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). Analysis is conducted by pre-training 1B LLaMA on C4 dataset. Optimizer rank r = 512 r=512 r = 128 r=128 r = 32 r=32 Optimizer State Peak Memory (GB) Adam 2.4942 2.4942 2.4942 ReLoRA [ 14 ] 1.1349 0.4670 0.3000 GaLore [ 39 ] 0.3385 0.3385 0.3385 OSD [ 15 ] 0.2832 0.2832 0.2832 Ori (Ours) 0.2583 0.2506 0.2487 Average Update Time (s / Step) Adam 12.6015 12.6015 12.6015 ReLoRA [ 14 ] 13.9454 11.9193 11.5661 GaLore [ 39 ] 12.9699 12.9703 13.0401 OSD [ 15 ] 12.8438 12.8373 12.8594 Ori (Ours) 12.7266 12.7206 12.6705 Table 10 : Memory and Wallclock Time Comparison between O-LDAdam and an error-feedback baseline, LDAdam. Analysis is conducted by pre-training 1B LLaMA on C4 dataset. Optimizer rank r = 512 r=512 r = 128 r=128 r = 32 r=32 Optimizer State Peak Memory (GB) LDAdam ( T = 1 T=1 ) 0.1221 0.1221 0.1221 LDAdam ( T = 200 T=200 ) 0.1221 0.1221 0.1221 O-LDAdam (Ours) 0.1221 0.1221 0.1221 Average Update Time (s / Step) LDAdam ( T = 1 T=1 ) 13.9294 13.3475 13.1410 LDAdam ( T = 200 T=200 ) 12.7141 12.6996 12.6863 O-LDAdam (Ours) 13.4735 12.9018 12.8648

We profile the optimizer state peak memory and wall-clock time during the pre-training experiments from Section 5.2 . Details on the memory profiling procedure can be found in Section E.8 . As shown in Table 9 , Ori exhibits a superior efficiency profile among standard, non-error-feedback gradient-subspace methods (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). In addition, as shown in Table 10 , O-LDAdam demonstrates competitive and comparable efficiency profile to the error-feedback baseline LDAdam under the large update frequency regime ( T = 200 T=200 ). Full table on pre-training of other model sizes can be found in Appendix F . Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. For instance, at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB). This confirms Ori’s tangible memory savings. On the other hand, compared to the error-feedback methods, O-LDAdam consistently yields the same memory footprint as LDAdam baselines. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

matches.title: Idea2Prior: Auditable Paper Retrieval and Ranking from Research Ideas
matches.abstract_excerpt: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present IDEA2PRIOR, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for IDEA2PRIOR, 43.3% for Cha

matches.title: From Relevance to Validity: Zero-Shot Tool Selection via Functional and Contextual Validation
matches.abstract_excerpt: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face tasks from unseen domains and execution contexts, making zero-shot tool selection essential for identifying tools that can satisfy task requirements. Existing dominant methods mainly rely on relevance ranking, but semantic matching alone cannot ensure that a tool is functionally compatible or remains applicable in a new context. We preliminarily identify a \emph{transfer-validity gap}, where semantically relevant tools may still fail to satisfy functional or contextual requirements after transfer. To address this gap, we propose \methodname{}, a progressive validation framework that complements semantic relevance with endpoint-grounded functional compatibility and task-conditioned contextual evidence. matches.title: Re-ranking and Late Interaction Drive Retrieval Quality: A Controlled Comparison of RAG Strategies for Scientific Question Answering
matches.abstract_excerpt: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is now the standard way to ground Large Language Models (LLMs) in external knowledge, yet the design space of retrieval pipelines is large and the trade-offs between variants are not well understood, especially on domain-specific corpora at realistic scale. matches.title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
matches.abstract_excerpt: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. matches.title: NoveltyScope: A Multi-Agent Research Assistant for Evidence-Grounded Novelty Assessment of Scientific Papers
matches.abstract_excerpt: NoveltyScope is a prototype that compares a scientific paper with retrieved prior work and produces a structured report and a five-level novelty score. The system extracts the core task and at most two author-claimed contributions, then searches a closed local corpus using BM25 and dense retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion. Contribution comparisons request paired passages for potential refutations, and quotations are checked against cached source text. Four scoring roles (Prosecutor, Defender, Judge, and Critic) use the resulting evidence, with at most one revision of the Judge's score. Evaluation uses 50 class-balanced RINoBench samples whose idea-level labels are retained for full-paper input. inspect:2610.31897.question: At matched model quality and compression ratio, how does jointly trained sparse-plus-low-rank compression compare with low-rank-only, sparsity-only, and post-training baselines on LLMs? What ablations isolate the low-rank component?

passages.text: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

Scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations ( Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2013 ; Gunn & Anderson, 2015 ) . Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Kuutti et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Bodmer et al., 2026 ) , while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded ( European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016 ; Shi et al., 2016 ) . These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety ( Shin & Cui, 1995 ; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004 ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Nan et al., 2026 ) .

To address memory constraints, existing compression methods use quantization ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , pruning ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank factorization ( Hsu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection 1 1 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1 ). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. Hardware-friendly patterns, including block sparsity ( Okanovic et al., 2025 ) , N : M N\!:\!M sparsity ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and row-/column-wise sparsity ( Wen et al., 2016 ) , are therefore required to translate these memory savings into efficient edge inference. A straightforward extension of SALAAD is to impose these patterns on its learned sparse components after pretraining. However, our experiments show that this post-hoc conversion can sharply degrade model performance (see Appendix A.2 ). We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining , allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

Compression methods for large language models broadly divide into pruning, low-rank factorization, and quantization. Unstructured pruning removes individual weights by magnitude ( Han et al., 2015 ) or calibration-based criteria ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ) , while low-rank methods such as SVD-LLM ( Wang et al., 2025c ) factorize weight matrices and SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) shrinks them by removing channels. A second post-hoc family instead runs iterative ADMM on the pretrained weights: ELSA ( Lee et al., 2026 ) pushes unstructured sparsity to extreme ratios, and 3BASiL ( Makni et al., 2025 ) performs layer-wise SLR reconstruction via a 3-block ADMM–both are data-hungry and take hours of GPU-time to compress a single model. Compression-aware pretraining instead induces compressibility during training: LORO ( Mo et al., 2025 ) pretrains in a preset low-rank subspace, SLTrain ( Han et al., 2024 ) augments low-rank pretraining with a fixed-support sparse component, and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) jointly learns SLR components via ADMM. The sparse components in SLTrain and SALAAD are unstructured and do not map efficiently onto accelerator primitives. LOST ( Li et al., 2025 ) combines low-rank factors with channel-wise sparsity, but its preset rank and sparse capacity fix the model size during training, and its formulation does not support elastic deployment across budgets from a single checkpoint. It also inserts an additional nonlinearity between the low-rank factors, changing the underlying model architecture. S-SALAAD preserves the original architecture and supports multiple structured sparsity patterns, learning a representation that can be compressed from a single checkpoint to different parameter budgets.

The L L -only variant is the S ≡ 0 S\equiv 0 special case of S-SALAAD. It retains ADMM’s coupled updates of X X and L L under the constraint X = L X\!=\!L , with the proximal update ( 8 ) explicitly removing small singular values from L L . This structure-learning procedure goes beyond directly adding a low-rank regularizer to the task loss. Figure 8 compares this variant with direct subgradient optimization of ℓ ⁡ ( X ) + λ ​ | X | ∗ \ell(X)\!+\!\lambda|X|_{*} . With λ = 10 − 6 \lambda\!=\!10^{-6} , perplexity is comparable to that of L L -only S-SALAAD at the largest budget but rises sharply as the budget decreases. This behavior is consistent with low-rank structure that is too weak to support aggressive compression. Increasing λ \lambda to 10 − 5 10^{-5} strengthens rank regularization and yields nearly constant perplexity across the tested budgets, supporting elastic compression at the cost of higher perplexity throughout. L L -only S-SALAAD maintains low perplexity over the same budget range, providing a better trade-off between model quality and elastic compressibility than these direct regularization baselines. Figure 8: Post-compression perplexity on Llama-350M.

Figures 9 and 10 compare I-SVD with exact SVD beyond the training-time results reported in the main text. I-SVD preserves both the post-compression validation perplexity and the effective-rank trajectories of exact SVD, confirming that the approximation does not degrade the learned decomposition. Figure 9: Post-compression perplexity for exact and iterative SVD on Llama-350M at matched budgets. (a) Layer 4. (b) Layer 8. (c) Layer 14. Figure 10: Γ L \Gamma_{L} trajectories for exact and iterative SVD on the down projections of three representative Llama-350M layers. Each inset magnifies the converged regime, where the two curves are otherwise indistinguishable.

inspect:2610.10965.question: In the NanoGPT experiments, which singular-value threshold variants match or outperform Muon on training speed and validation loss, and how do they change the effective rank of weight matrices? What controlled comparisons support these findings?

passages.text: Figure 3 (a) shows that the singular values are spread across many orders of magnitude, indicating that gradient matrices in the language model setting are very poorly conditioned. This variation does not stem from variation between different matrices: as we can see in Figure 4 (a), the effective rank of the gradient stays below about 280 for most of training. This implies a low-entropy and highly nonuniform distribution within each matrix. Figure 3 (a) also displays the distribution of the gradients after Nesterov momentum is applied. Momentum thins out the low end of the spectrum, suggesting that it suppresses some noisy directions, but otherwise leaves its shape alone and simply shifts scale. This distribution was used to select the absolute thresholds τ \tau for targeted Muon. Averaged over matrices, the top arm lifts about 1% to 28% of the singular directions, and the bottom arm lifts from nearly all of the directions down to about 30%. In terms of squared Frobenius norm, the lifted band holds 32–96% of the momentum in the top arm and at most 13% in the bottom arm. Note that τ \tau is absolute while the bulk of the spectrum sits at different levels in different matrices, so the same τ \tau lifts very different fractions of different matrices. In the top arm this compounds: a matrix whose spectrum falls below τ \tau only gets its raw momentum and effectively stops training, so at the larger thresholds most of the deeper layers are left untouched. Also note that every momentum singular value is far below one, so the targeted region is always amplified, not suppressed.

Validation loss was monitored throughout and remained almost exactly at training loss, so overfitting is not a concern. Every Muon variant drops the loss faster than AdamW over the first hundred steps (Figure 3 (b)), and the lead grows with how much of the spectrum is lifted. Lifting only the top few directions with a high τ \tau already gets much of Muon’s early advantage, but the lead reverses within a few hundred steps, and every top dose ends up behind AdamW with warmup, the smallest ones even behind NSGD (Table 1 ). This is not a matter of step size. Raising the learning rate of the top variants only makes them worse and collapses their rank further (Figure 5 (c)), while Muon at a tenth of its learning rate loses just 0.05. Figure 3 (c,d) plots the final loss against τ \tau and against the fraction of the momentum that is orthogonalized. For both top and bottom targeting, loss falls monotonically with the portion of directions orthogonalized. However, the two arms are not symmetric. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix gets within 0.03 of Muon while orthogonalizing only about 13% of the momentum matrix’s magnitude, while lifting only the top directions remains well short even when they make up 96% of it, and the smallest top doses do worse than lifting nothing. This answers one part of our original question. Despite being a very small portion of the momentum magnitude, the small singular values are not noise. The model can be usefully trained on them, but only once they are amplified to full scale. (a) Gradient effective rank (b) Update effective rank (c) Value matrix effective rank (d) Output matrix effective rank (e) MLP effective rank

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (a) Tangent alignment (b) Spectrum-changing update by singular direction (c) Final loss vs. parameter rank

Figure 5: How much of the update changes the spectrum, and where. (a) Log-barrier of the isospectral tangent fraction, averaged over matrices; the grey dotted line is the value for a random rotation, the orange dotted line marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and dashed lines are the warmup variants. (b) Share of the spectrum-changing part of the update at each singular direction of the parameter, ranked by singular value, averaged over matrices and steps 100–1500; the dotted line is uniform. (c) Final validation loss against final parameter effective rank, including the learning rate controls; the bottom-targeted runs at τ ≤ 4 × 10 − 4 \tau\leq 4\times 10^{-4} leave their MLP output matrices barely trained. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Intuitively, an update that keeps pushing along the leading singular directions of a matrix reinforces what is already there, while a full-spectrum update mostly rotates the basis and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Figure 5 (c) plots these against the final loss. Figure 5 (a) shows the same thing with the isospectral tangent metric of Section 3.3 . Every optimizer puts more of its update into the parameter’s own basis than a random update would, and tangent alignment rises for every optimizer over training, fastest during the cooldown. Among the targeted variants of Muon, the bottom targeted versions show higher alignment than Muon, while the top targeted versions show lower alignment. This is reversed compared to the CIFAR experiments, but it reveals the same underlying phenomenon. In the NanoGPT domain, the targeted region has its magnitude raised, while the remaining regions are relatively suppressed. Therefore, it is simply the top few directions of the gradient which lie within the existing basis of the parameter, and the more you shrink them in the update, the less poorly conditioned the parameter matrices become. Note that structure and performance don’t move together: AdamW collapses rank and still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. This suggests that keeping the spectrum flat is

From our experiments on NanoGPT, we concluded that the small singular values of the momentum are not noise but directions the model can feasibly train on once they are amplified. Orthogonalizing everything but the few largest singular values nearly matches Muon, while orthogonalizing only the top buys an early lead over AdamW and then falls behind even normalized SGD. Keeping the top from dominating the update is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; the tangent alignment shows that the top singular directions are the ones that lie outside the tangent space of the isospectral manifold, so they are what changes the spectrum. This is cheap, however, and is not what drives the loss, as AdamW collapses rank and still performs well. AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, because an elementwise normalized update must build a matrix out of many low rank steps, where an orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step. This explains AdamW’s slower start and why warmup helps it but hurts Muon. Finally, the effective rank of the gradient becomes an effective tool to determine position in the loss landscape, and also shows the difference between optimizers in where the early steps take the parameters.

(a) Gradient effective rank (b) Update effective rank (c) Value matrix effective rank (d) Output matrix effective rank (e) MLP effective rank

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (a) Tangent alignment (b) Spectrum-changing update by singular direction (c) Final loss vs. parameter rank

Figure 5: How much of the update changes the spectrum, and where. (a) Log-barrier of the isospectral tangent fraction, averaged over matrices; the grey dotted line is the value for a random rotation, the orange dotted line marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and dashed lines are the warmup variants. (b) Share of the spectrum-changing part of the update at each singular direction of the parameter, ranked by singular value, averaged over matrices and steps 100–1500; the dotted line is uniform. (c) Final validation loss against final parameter effective rank, including the learning rate controls; the bottom-targeted runs at τ ≤ 4 × 10 − 4 \tau\leq 4\times 10^{-4} leave their MLP output matrices barely trained. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Intuitively, an update that keeps pushing along the leading singular directions of a matrix reinforces what is already there, while a full-spectrum update mostly rotates the basis and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Figure 5 (c) plots these against the final loss. Figure 5 (a) shows the same thing with the isospectral tangent metric of Section 3.3 . Every optimizer puts more of its update into the parameter’s own basis than a random update would, and tangent alignment rises for every optimizer over training, fastest during the cooldown. Among the targeted variants of Muon, the bottom targeted versions show higher alignment than Muon, while the top targeted versions show lower alignment. This is reversed compared to the CIFAR experiments, but it reveals the same underlying phenomenon. In the NanoGPT domain, the targeted region has its magnitude raised, while the remaining regions are relatively suppressed. Therefore, it is simply the top few directions of the gradient which lie within the existing basis of the parameter, and the more you shrink them in the update, the less poorly conditioned the parameter matrices become. Note that structure and performance don’t move together: AdamW collapses rank and still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. This suggests that keeping the spectrum flat is

From our experiments on NanoGPT, we concluded that the small singular values of the momentum are not noise but directions the model can feasibly train on once they are amplified. Orthogonalizing everything but the few largest singular values nearly matches Muon, while orthogonalizing only the top buys an early lead over AdamW and then falls behind even normalized SGD. Keeping the top from dominating the update is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; the tangent alignment shows that the top singular directions are the ones that lie outside the tangent space of the isospectral manifold, so they are what changes the spectrum. This is cheap, however, and is not what drives the loss, as AdamW collapses rank and still performs well. AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, because an elementwise normalized update must build a matrix out of many low rank steps, where an orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step. This explains AdamW’s slower start and why warmup helps it but hurts Muon. Finally, the effective rank of the gradient becomes an effective tool to determine position in the loss landscape, and also shows the difference between optimizers in where the early steps take the parameters.

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

The rise is not (mostly) miscalibration. Fitting a temperature on a held-out clean split never used for training ( Guo et al., 2017 ) leaves 83 % 83\% of the noisy cliff standing ( 0.44 0.44 vs. 0.53 0.53 nats, 5 5 seeds), rescaling leaves the accuracy drop unchanged, and expected calibration error, Brier score and selective-risk area all degrade across the same range ( Naeini et al., 2015 ; Brier, 1950 ; Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017 ; Geifman et al., 2019 ) . With clean labels calibration removes about half the rise instead (Table 12 ). Under label noise, the cliff is mostly real error rather than overconfidence. Noise and augmentation change only the cliff’s depth. CIFAR-100N human re-annotation labels ( Wei et al., 2022 ) replicate the cliff with larger amplitude. Sweeping η ∈ { 10 , 20 , 40 , 60 } % \eta\in\{10,20,40,60\}\% keeps the valley pinned at r = 1 r{=}1 while the amplitude grows monotonically, and augmentation shrinks the amplitude without changing the shape or adding a second descent (Appendix E.1 ). The peak moves with the training budget. From 40 40 to 80 80 epochs it shifts from r = 64 r{=}64 to r = 32 r{=}32 , and at 20 20 epochs risk is monotone in rank because low ranks have not yet interpolated. The peak reflects interpolation status at the current budget ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) , so the protocol locates r interp r_{\mathrm{interp}} per budget. Neither longer training nor α / r \alpha/r scaling returns the tail to the valley (Appendix B.1 ).

Model selection shrinks the cliff without removing it. Selecting learning rate, weight decay and stopping epoch on a clean validation split reduces the cliff from 0.53 0.53 to 0.16 0.16 nats. The selected models retain the rank ordering on fresh seeds, and every selected checkpoint precedes interpolation (Appendix E.2 ), which is the mechanism: selection escapes the cliff by declining to interpolate, not by crossing it. Because per-rank selection includes no dense arm, it bears on the shape of the axis and not on the gap to dense. No tested setting removes the cliff once ranks interpolate. Corrupting the frozen backbone only deepens the cliff, and its shape persists through changes in data size, learning rate, weight decay, scaling, adapter placement and dataset (Appendices C.2 , E.1 and E.3 ; Table 15 ). Architecture decides too. A ResNet completes the descent on these subsets; a width-scaled ViT trained from scratch does not (Appendix B.2 ), recovering 0.56 0.56 of 3.23 3.23 nats, the final-ascent regime of Xue et al. (2024) . Dense-block fine-tuning of a transformer reaches Rec = 0.82 \mathrm{Rec}{=}0.82 , so the rank axis’s shallow far side is not a transformer property. Scope. The experiments cover noisy image and text classification with AdamW, synthetic and human label noise, and budgets up to 160 160 epochs. The dense reference is module-matched, training the projections LoRA adapts rather than the whole network; the dense-block axis of Section 5.5 unfreezes up to six full blocks. Test NLL is the primary measurement, and accuracy follows its ordering inside the parameter-saving window but can diverge at larger ranks. Where LoRA crosses dense depends on the protocol and the grid.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

passages.text: The 7 7 B rank axis is the clearest case for reading the tail against a module-matched baseline rather than against the pre-peak valley. Every sampled rank, parity included, remains behind dense in all three seeds, while the valley reference reads Rec > 1 \mathrm{Rec}>1 at every sampled rank from r = 448 r{=}448 on. Setup. Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) , with d = 3584 d{=}3584 and grouped-query attention with key and value width 512 512 , is fine-tuned for sequence classification on 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) with 20 % 20\% symmetric label noise, sequence length 128 128 , a freshly initialized linear head, AdamW at lr 6.6 × 10 − 5 6.6\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} , batch 16 16 , 20 20 epochs, bfloat16. LoRA wraps the query, key and value projections of the last six blocks as three separate modules, so the adapter trains 15,360 ​ r 15{,}360r parameters per block against dense’s 16,515,072 16{,}515{,}072 and parity falls at r ≈ 1075 r{\approx}1075 . The dense arm trains the weights of those projections and freezes their biases, as does LoRA. Both arms train the same classification head with the same optimizer settings. Seeds control the subset, the noise draw, the head init and the adapter init, and are shared across arms, so the differences below are paired. Each run takes about an hour on one A100, and the r = 512 r{=}512 and r = 900 r{=}900 runs take under an hour each on one RTX 5090 under identical settings. In the table, srank \mathrm{srank} is the stable rank ‖ Δ ​ W ‖ F 2 / ‖ Δ ​ W ‖ 2 2 \|\Delta W\|_{F}^{2}/\|\Delta W\|_{2}^{2} of the update, averaged over adapted modules.

How are the 68.9-to-52.9 GB peak-memory and 1288-to-304 ms optimizer-step results measured, and what are the corresponding validation losses?

passages.text: Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. Full-step measurements capture this crossover, which optimizer-step timings alone would miss. Table 2 : Training costs on one H100 at microbatch 4, indexed by the dense reference model size. Monarch–Muon uses 4 blocks. Top: peak allocated memory and optimizer buffers, including projection matrices (GB). Low precision reduces the bytes and arithmetic cost of the representation that Monarch has already compressed. Following the FP8 approach of COAT ( Xi et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate two separate extensions of the two-block dense quality model: FP8 factor GEMMs with compressed activations, and FP8 optimizer buffers with BF16 GEMMs. Both use the same 39,250-step training recipe, with final loss evaluated in BF16 (Appendix A.5 ). The FP8 computation and activation recipe preserves the optimizer ordering while reducing peak memory by about 31% and training-step time by 14% for Monarch–Muon. Final loss remains within 0.23% of BF16 for both optimizers (Table 5 ). Quantizing optimizer buffers separately gives nearly unchanged loss and reduces their storage by 3.7 × 3.7\times . These results show two complementary uses of low precision: reducing the larger activation footprint and further compressing the already smaller optimizer state. Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. inspect:2610.04249.question: Which balance and alignment assumptions are required for the singular-mode results, and what experiments compare GD, SignGD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC on weight spectra, effective rank, and model quality?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

We first evaluate the optimizer dependent spectral dynamics in the full observation matrix factorization setting described in App. F , where the theoretical phase laws apply most directly. Figure 4: Optimizer geometry sets the pace of spectral learning evaluation in matrix factorization. (a) Evolution of a weak target mode with μ = 0.18 \mu=0.18 , shown as the learned fraction σ ⁡ ( t ) / μ \sigma(t)/\mu . GD exhibits the factorization induced small mode barrier, whereas normalization and preconditioning substantially accelerate emergence. (b) Birth time to the common amplitude b = 0.03 b=0.03 as the target mode μ \mu varies. While ideal Muon is independent of the target mode ordering during birth, other optimizers are target sensitive. (c) Decay trajectories for an unsupported mode with target μ = 0 \mu=0 . Ideal Muon removes the mode in finite time, undamped K-FAC produces exponential decay, while GD, instantaneous Adam with fixed stabilization, and cumulative Shampoo retain increasingly slow tails near zero. Optimizer geometry therefore determines which spectral components emerge, persist, and disappear.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Figure 5: Optimization and rank dynamics in matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

We next consider a less structured setting in which the effective predictor is trained by underdetermined linear regression as described in App. F . This experiment tests whether the qualitative predictions persist once our simplifying assumptions Assumptions 1 , 2 and 3 are removed. Fig. 16 shows that the optimizers reach comparable training losses and converge to nearly identical final singular spectra. This agreement is important: the pronounced differences observed during training are not simply consequences of one method converging to a substantially different level of fit. Nevertheless, the stable and effective ranks evolve differently. Thus similar terminal predictors need not imply similar spectral learning dynamics. Figure 16: Optimizer dependent dynamics persist in underdetermined linear regression. We train the same deep linear predictor on an underdetermined, nonwhitened regression problem using GD, Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and KFAC. All methods reach comparable final loss and final spectra of W W despite substantially different transient dynamics shown by the stable rank and effective rank throughout training. The optimizer geometry strongly changes how quickly spectral mass concentrates.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 17 make this distinction particularly clear. GD exhibits pronounced separation between the emergence times of successive singular values, consistent with the factorization induced small mode barrier derived in the aligned setting. Adam substantially compresses these delays. Muon produces a markedly more synchronized growth of the singular spectrum, consistent with normalization reducing mode dependent mobility differences. Cumulative Shampoo also accelerates weaker spectral components after its preconditioner has accumulated sufficient history, while K-FAC produces comparatively smooth growth across the spectrum through curvature correction. These effects remain visible even though the singular vectors are not fixed and the data covariance couples the modes. The experiment therefore supports the interpretation of the theoretical phase laws as mechanisms governing transient spectral learning rather than merely properties of the special aligned model. Exact exponents depend on the aligned reduction, but the resulting qualitative distinctions persist in the more practical underdetermined regression problem. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 17: Singular value trajectories in nonaligned underdetermined linear regression. Although all methods approach similar final singular spectra, their transient spectrum differ substantially. The qualitative optimizer dependent dynamics predicted by the aligned phase analysis remain visible even when the empirical data covariance couples singular directions and the exact scalar mode reduction no longer holds.

inspect:2611.07859.question: In the controlled closed-search evaluations, what are CORE's exact answer-accuracy and evidence-recall results against Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher, and which ablations isolate snippet selection, context expansion, and duplicate suppression while holding the agent model and corpus fixed?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

BrowseComp-Plus CM requires searching 553 million ClimbMix documents, our largest corpus. CORE again leads in both accuracy and recall for every agent. Its advantage is most pronounced with Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B. CORE outperforms OpenResearcher by 14.03 points. With GPT-5.4, CORE raises accuracy to 68.42%, compared with 56.14% for OpenResearcher and 50.88% for Tongyi DeepResearch. With Qwen3.8-27B, Tongyi DeepResearch is the stronger baseline in accuracy, and CORE still exceeds both baselines in accuracy and recall.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

passages.section: A.3 Selection of the Deep Research Agent
passages.text: We compare Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B and OpenResearcher-30B-A3B ( Li et al., 2026b ) under CORE on BrowseComp-Plus. Both use the same corpus, passage index, retrieval and context-management configuration, and GPT-5.5 judge at high reasoning effort. Sampling parameters follow Appendix A.2 ; context budgets and tool-call formats follow each model’s configuration. Table 3 shows higher answer accuracy for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B in this setting, supporting its selection for the main experiments. Accuracy is computed over all 830 questions; empty answers receive no credit. Bold marks the higher accuracy.

In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.
